Isaac Lab 3.0 · PhysX · two to four Franka arms

MRMem: a benchmark where memory is provably necessary for cooperating robots

Long-horizon manipulation tasks for teams of two to four robots (a pharmacy, a workshop, a kitchen, a stove, a warehouse, a lab bench, an assembly line), in which one robot perceives something, time passes, and later one of them must act on it. Every evaluation episode comes with a counterfactual twin that is identical except for what had to be remembered, so a policy without memory cannot pass.

4 × 4 memory type × who perceives the cue 8 tasks with 2, 3 and 4 arms 128/128 grid cells certified (8 tasks × 16) bit-exact twins across processes per-robot observation boundaries
Memory type × who perceives the cue Click a cell to see the tasks of that kind
What the rows and columns mean
Rows: what must be remembered (RoboMME's memory types)
Permanence (where): an item was put into one of three lidded containers; once the lids are on, every container looks the same. The decider must open the one the item went into.
Reference (which): a robot is told which container an item belongs in; when it later stores the item, nothing in view encodes the instruction.
Imitation (in what order): three items are stored in an instructed order; the decider must take them out in the same order (the twins differ only in the order).
Counting (how many times): a tool is dipped into an open container one, two or three times; the decider must dip it as often (one more fails).
Columns: who perceives the cue (information distribution)
Decider: only the robot that later decides: it is told and acts itself (stores, doses), and later uses its own memory. The other robots do not see it.
Shared: the decider and its partner both perceive it (the decider watches the partner store, or both are told).
Partner: only the partner perceives it; the decider looks away and learns it only if the partner tells it with its own message action.
Communicated: only the partner perceives it; the decider looks away, and a message tells it later (it must remember the message).

In every cell, each task's counterfactual twins are certified: the twins differ only in what had to be remembered, the decider's current observation is identical in both at the decision, the expert solves every pair, a decider without memory none, and a decider told the answer every pair. A cell's number counts the tasks certified in it; the dots are the six container cells. Partner and communicated episodes are physically the shared ones (only what the decider perceives differs), so they show the shared clip, marked =.

What the dataset has that others do not

Built for long-horizon multi-robot memory

Single-robot memory benchmarks such as RoboMME define the memory types; task-state benchmarks such as MAGMA add interruptions and errors; multi-robot benchmarks such as RoboFactory add cooperation. MRMem combines all three, and it checks every evaluation episode for memory necessity instead of assuming it.

Certified necessity

Counterfactual twin pairs

Each pair differs only in the remembered fact. The verifier proves that the decider's current observation is identical in both twins when it must act, and that the correct actions differ.

Information boundaries

One observation group per robot

Each robot sees its own proprioception, objects in plain view from its own base, and its own notifications. Tests reject any term that reads the partner's state.

Ground truth

Memory labels per decision

decider_informed, requires_communication, cue_carrier, and the fact version the decider knows, so every failure is labelled valid, stale or missing memory.

Provenance

Semantic event log

Every event records who caused it, who perceived it and which event led to it. Any state change can be traced back to its origin.

No hidden channels

Per-agent causality check

A robot may act differently only after its own observations differ. The partner may not move differently before the decider does, so motion cannot carry the answer.

Controls

Memory-free twins on the same seeds

Persistent cues, or see-through containers in the kitchen, give the answer at decision time. They separate memory failures from motor failures.

Physical hiding

Closed drawers hide the item

In the kitchen the jar disappears behind a drawer front. The answer is not a symbol that stays on screen, so the visuomotor variant also needs memory.

Task state

Interruptions and execution errors

MAGMA-style conditions insert a service subtask during retention or make the jar slip after it is taken out. Each perturbed episode has a clean control with the same seed.

Decision metric

Offline decision probe

Policies read the recorded twin observations and predict the decider's action where the expert's actions first part. This measures memory without the noise of closed-loop motor failures.

Task families

Two scenes, the same memory machinery

Bimanual bar handoff

Robot A lifts a bar and hands it to B in mid-air; B places it in one of three slots on its side. With several legs, the roles alternate. The decision is the slot.

Memory typeHow the answer arrives
ReferenceAn instruction names the slot
Countingn identical pulses: slot n
PermanenceA token at the slot, then occluded
ImitationOne demonstration of all legs, in order

Kitchen storage

A cabinet with two drawers and a two-door compartment stands between the robots. A stores a jar; later B must fetch it. The decision is the first container B opens, so the answer changes the whole retrieval motion.

Memory typeEpisodeStatus
PermanenceB watches A store the jarcertified
ReferenceA is told where to store itcertified
UpdatesInstruction replaced; or changed and heard by B onlycertified
CountingA opens and closes a drawer n times; B repeats it n timescertified
ImitationTwo identical jars; B fetches the one A stored firstcertified
Memory setups

Four axes, set independently of the manipulation

Every task takes a memory type and three axes. The generator places the cue events on the episode's subtask timeline and labels each decision with what the decider can know. Pick a setup to see who perceives what and which policies can solve it.

Memory type
Retention
Distribution
Update

Cooperation setups

From sequential help to co-manipulation and messages

Cooperation grows in steps. Each step keeps the certification: the twins still differ only in the remembered fact, and causality is still checked per robot.

Bimanual bar handoff

certified

Both robots hold the same bar at once during the handover. The receiver decides where the bar goes.

Store, then retrieve

kitchen phase 1

A stores the jar while B watches; after the retention gap B fetches it. B's memory comes from A's actions: A is the cue_carrier.

Learned messages

certified

In the partner setting B never sees the storage. With A's message it opens the right drawer in every episode (50% without), and all 24 pairs pass certification with messages counted as B's observations. A discrete message action m ∈ {0…K}. The partner receives it as a notification on the same step, and the log records the sender. This makes the partner and stale setups solvable by decentralized policies.

Held drawers

certified

Drawers close on a spring (20 N/m, about 4.8 N at the storage opening). One robot holds the drawer while the other puts the jar in or takes it out. With robot A parked, B opens the right drawer in 8 of 8 episodes and succeeds in none: the task needs both robots.

Private compartments

planned

A door compartment is reachable only by its owner. When the jar is in A's compartment and B must deliver it, the robots have to coordinate a retrieval or a handover.

Dataset format

What each episode records

One HDF5 file per run, in the Isaac Lab recorder layout, extended with what memory research needs. This is a real kitchen episode (1778 steps).

data/demo_0/
  actions                 (1778, 16)   # both robots, columns per agent in the file attributes
  obs/robot_a/            # what robot A may use, and nothing else
    joint_pos, ee_pose, gripper, finger_force, last_arm_action …
    item                  (1778, 4)    # visible flag + jar position in A's base frame; 0 when hidden
    openings              (1778, 5)    # visible flag + four container openings
    notifications         (1778, 44)   # events A perceives, one step each
    cues                  (1778, 4)    # non-zero only in memory-free controls
  obs/robot_b/            # the same terms for robot B
  obs/state               (1778, 69)   # privileged; critics, experts, evaluation only
  event_log/              # step, type, source, entity, visible-to mask, fact, old/new, cause
  task/
    status, assignee      # subtask state per step
    fact_value, fact_version, belief_version   # truth vs. what each robot knows
  scenario/
    pair, twin, twin_group  # counterfactual pair membership
    decision_step, decision_truth, decision_belief
    persistent_cues, condition, seed
  states/, initial_state/   # full articulation and object state, for replay
# file attributes: task spec, memory axes, generated events, decision labels, expert belief layout

In partner setups the decider never perceives the answer, so the expert is at chance by design. In reference · immediate the instruction first arrived on the same step as the start signal and the memoryless decider solved every pair; the signal now comes 35 steps later, as in the bar task.

Learned policies: who carries the memory

Behaviour cloning on expert demonstrations (1024 per bar configuration, 256 in the kitchen), one policy per robot reading only its own observations. The table counts pairs the offline probe discriminates, out of 32 (bar handoff) or 8 (kitchen). Only a policy that remembers can discriminate a pair.

ConfigurationMemorylessHistory MLP
(last 64 steps)		GRUTransformer

The history MLP solves exactly the immediate setups, whose gap fits its 64-step window. The Transformer discriminates 32/32 everywhere except imitation (10/32), and 8/8 in the kitchen. The GRU did not learn the long dependency in 10,000 training steps.
